# Annotations and catalogues

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/09-catalogs.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
:::

Long reads showed that many unannotated transcripts are real, without settling
what a reference annotation is for, and that second question is now the harder
one. Depth alone could inflate reference transcript sets by millions of models,
so the decision facing every catalogue is editorial rather than technical
[@monzo2025challenges].

## MANE and APPRIS: one transcript per gene {#sec-mane}

Clinical reporting needed a default transcript and had none. MANE Select names
exactly one representative transcript per human protein-coding gene, identical
in exon structure between Ensembl/GENCODE and RefSeq [@morales2022mane].

When the two annotation groups
first compared their independent choices, they agreed on the same transcript
for only 14 per cent of protein-coding genes [@morales2022mane]. By the June
2021 release MANE had a Select transcript for 97 per cent of human
protein-coding genes, 18,584 of them, including every gene on the ACMG
secondary-findings list [@morales2022mane].

The exception was designed in from the start. MANE Plus Clinical exists for the
small set of loci where pathogenic variants fall on exons the Select transcript
omits, and at first release covered 55 genes [@morales2022mane]. That set
grows as pathogenic variants accumulate, reaching 64 transcripts by release v47
[@mudge2024gencode].

Those authors also pre-empted the obvious misreading. Picking one transcript
per locus is not a claim that a gene's biology reduces to that transcript, and
tissue- and development-specific isoform diversity is outside the set's scope
[@morales2022mane].

APPRIS reaches a single principal isoform by a different route, from protein
evidence rather than expression: mapped structures, functional domains,
conserved residues and cross-species alignment [@rodriguez2021appris]. The two
routes largely converge, agreeing for over 97 per cent of coding genes, though
not independently, because APPRIS principal isoforms are themselves an input to
MANE Select curation [@rodriguez2021appris].

![Four ways of choosing one transcript, scored against what proteomics finds
dominant. The two convenience heuristics are the ones people reach for when no
curated set is to hand.](../figures/representative-transcript.svg){#fig-representative width=100%}

Benchmarking against the dominant isoform in proteomics puts numbers on the cost
of the shortcuts. Agreement was about 96.1 per cent for APPRIS core principal
isoforms and 94.6 per cent for MANE Select. The convenience heuristics gave 86.4
per cent for simply taking the longest isoform and 70.1 per cent for taking the
most-expressed transcript. Those four rates are computed over different gene
subsets, and a randomly chosen isoform agreed about 30 per cent of the time
[@pozo2022appris].

Expression is a worse guide than its popularity suggests, and long reads agree.
Of 18,083 genes matched between MANE and long-read GTEx data, 13,245 MANE
Select transcripts were also the top-expressed protein-coding transcript
[@tung2022texmst]. Those authors read that as MANE dominance. It also leaves a
substantial remainder, part of which reflects transcript-ID mismatch between
the GENCODE releases used rather than real disagreement about which isoform is
highest [@tung2022texmst].

## GENCODE grows by revision as well as addition {#sec-gencode}

GENCODE's human and mouse annotation was originally produced by human curators
working locus by locus along each chromosome, and only became project-based
once that first full pass was finished [@mudge2024gencode].

Long reads entered through targeted capture sequencing plus a supervised
workflow, TAGENE, built so that machine-generated transcript models could reach
close to manual-curation quality at scale [@mudge2024gencode]. The effect
landed almost entirely on one biotype. Long-read capture added over 140,000 new
human and 132,000 new mouse lncRNA transcript models in a single annotation
generation, which the project describes as roughly three-fold and six-fold
increases [@mudge2024gencode].

Annotation is not purely additive, and over the same period more than 37,000
existing human and mouse models were modified, while protein-coding counts moved
only incrementally [@mudge2024gencode].

The instability is long-standing and has been quantified. Across the first 24
GENCODE releases, only 54,840 of the 251,614 transcript models ever annotated,
about 21.7 per cent, kept the same annotation in every release. Biotype
reassignment and outright deletion affected the rest [@jalali2016gencode]. Over
those same releases the human transcript count grew from 87,852 to 199,005, and
most of the added models were not protein-coding. Protein-coding models went
from 43,415 at v1 to 79,865 at V24, alongside 119,140 transcripts of other
biotypes at V24 [@jalali2016gencode].

GENCODE is candid about what it does and does not know. Its coding-isoform
annotation is deliberately permissive, since an alternative transcript is
generally tagged as coding when translation is mechanistically plausible. The
project is confident about which genes are protein-coding and much less so
about which isoforms are [@mudge2024gencode]. It also expects per-gene
transcript counts in the tens to hundreds to become normal, and states plainly
that many of those transcripts will have unknown function
[@mudge2024gencode].

The response was a filtered view rather than a smaller catalogue. GENCODE
Primary takes every MANE Select and MANE Plus Clinical transcript plus a
minimal computationally selected remainder. It averages two transcripts per
protein-coding gene in its first human release and became the default browser
view, while the full comprehensive set stays available
[@mudge2024gencode].

## The long-read catalogues {#sec-encode4}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Both long-read catalogues here are preprints

The ENCODE4 long-read collection and the GTEx long-read transcriptome appear in
this book's corpus only as preprints, and the bibliography emits them as such.
Numbers taken from either need re-checking against the peer-reviewed version.
:::

ENCODE4 built its long-read transcriptome from 264 PacBio libraries drawn from
81 human and mouse tissue or cell-line samples. Those reduce to 49 unique
tissues or cell types once mouse developmental time-points are collapsed
[@reese2023encode4].

In the human data, 206,806 transcripts from polyadenylated genes were detected
at or above 1 TPM. Of those, 76,469, about 37 per cent, used an exon junction
chain annotated in neither GENCODE v29 nor v40 [@reese2023encode4]. Novelty was
unevenly distributed across the three structural axes described in
@sec-three-axes: splice patterns were far more often unannotated than
transcript start or end sites [@reese2023encode4].

The result those authors put against single-representative-transcript resources
is the dominance one. Across the sample panel, nearly three quarters of human
protein-coding genes did not have one stable top-expressed transcript, because
which isoform dominated changed with the tissue or cell line
[@reese2023encode4]. They framed the work as a direct challenge to that
assumption, naming it explicitly before testing it [@reese2023encode4].

That three-quarters figure sits above the one in @sec-how-functional, where
about 35 per cent of genes switch which transcript dominates between tissues
[@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript]. The two numbers are measuring different
things. The earlier one counts genes whose dominant transcript changes between
primary tissues in short-read data. This one counts genes with no single top
transcript stable across a long-read panel that includes cell lines. Neither is
wrong, and quoting either without its panel is.

Other catalogues give the same shape at different scales. The GTEx long-read
survey covered 88 samples on Nanopore and added just under 100,000 previously
unannotated transcripts to already-annotated genes [@glinos2021transcriptome].
In that dataset 127,478 transcripts were quantified across 27,461 genes, and 77
per cent had intron chains matching nothing in the GENCODE release used. Intron
retention was strongly enriched among the novel set [@glinos2021transcriptome].

The TRAILS immune atlas catalogued 159,369 isoforms from 17,496 loci across 29
human immune cell subsets. Of those, 78 per cent carried either a novel
splice-site combination or an outright novel splice site relative to GENCODE
[@inamo2024trails]. It also reports its own ceiling, since the whole atlas comes
from one healthy donor. A single independent PBMC sample from a second
individual reproduced 85.0 per cent of the isoforms expressed in PBMC, and only
30.6 per cent of the catalogued isoforms across all cell types. That is why the
resource ships as both an exploratory and a validated set [@inamo2024trails].

Non-human catalogues start lower and behave the same. One multiplexed Nanopore
run over 32 bovine tissues yielded 99,044 transcript isoforms at 31,824 loci.
Only 21 per cent exactly matched an existing reference transcript, while 61 per
cent were novel isoforms of known genes [@halstead2021bovine].

### Ancestry and the annotation gap

A diverse-ancestry long-read cohort collapsed 380,519 candidate transcript
models to 155,875 after reproducibility filtering. Of those, 41,297 were novel
and 31,097 were absent from the GTEx, ENCODE4 and CHESS3 catalogues
[@clavellrevelles2025ancestry].

The gap is not ancestry-neutral, because population-specific transcripts found
only in European samples were enriched for already-annotated structures, while
those found only in non-European samples were enriched for novel ones
[@clavellrevelles2025ancestry]. The annotation is a record of who has been
sequenced.

## Novel means absent from one chosen reference {#sec-what-novel-means}

Novelty defined against an evolving annotation is circular, because a
transcript can be called novel purely for not yet having been curated into a
release [@zheng2026isopedia].

Isopedia makes recurrence the unit of evidence instead. It indexes long-read
alignments from 1,007 public human transcriptomes, 603 PacBio and 404 Nanopore,
across 37 tissue contexts [@zheng2026isopedia].

Changing the denominator changes the answer by more than an order of magnitude.
One benchmark sample was re-scored against a population of long-read
transcriptomes instead of against a reference annotation. Its apparent novel
fraction fell from roughly 27 to 52 per cent down to 2 to 5 per cent, a
reduction of up to 26-fold [@zheng2026isopedia]. The transcripts are the same in
both scorings, and only the question changed.

## LRGASP: length for structure, depth for abundance {#sec-lrgasp}

LRGASP was a community exercise rather than one lab's comparison. Participants
worked from a shared body of over 427 million long reads spanning cDNA and
direct-RNA protocols in human, mouse and manatee. The study design was
published as a Registered Report in advance, and scoring was done by organisers
who had not submitted predictions [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp].

Its headline result separates the two jobs long reads get used for. Read length
and accuracy drive correct transcript structures, while raw depth drives
accurate abundance estimates, so one library design cannot be optimal for both
[@pardopalacios2024lrgasp].

The reproducibility numbers across pipelines are stark. In one human cell line
nearly 280,000
novel isoforms were reported in total, of which only 743 were called
consistently across pipelines, while 242,125 were seen by only one or two
[@pardopalacios2024lrgasp].

Low reproducibility did not mean the transcripts were false. Targeted PCR
validated all consistently detected novel isoforms, and still validated 90 per
cent of poorly reproducible novel-in-catalog isoforms and 50 per cent of
novel-not-in-catalog ones [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp]. Pipelines disagree about
which novel isoforms to report, and the ones they report are frequently real.

Without a reference annotation, tool choice swamps biology. De novo submissions
on the same mouse sample reported between roughly 20,000 and 150,000
transcripts, and on the manatee sample between roughly 2,000 and 500,000. The
consortium's verdict was that de novo annotation remains challenging and needs
further tool development [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp].

Their standing recommendation is procedural rather than tool-specific:
high-quality data, biological replicates, extensive orthogonal evidence, a
transcript-level filter, and transcripts identified by more than one analysis
tool [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp].

## Catalogue size is a policy choice {#sec-per-gene-counts}

Short-read assembly reached the opposite verdict about transcriptional
abundance. Assembling thousands of GTEx samples produced over 30 million
distinct transcripts at some 700,000 genomic locations, of which those authors
judged only about 42,000, six per cent, to be functional gene loci
[@pertea2018chess].

The successor catalogue shows what an inclusion rule does to a number. By
excluding anything judged non-functional, CHESS 3 lists 19,839 protein-coding
genes with 99,202 transcripts, about five per gene, against roughly 110,000
protein-coding transcripts in the contemporaneous GENCODE release
[@varabyou2023chess3]. The gene counts agree, while the transcript counts
diverge because the projects are answering different questions.

A single right annotation is incoherent as a goal, because the uses conflict.
Maximal transcript representation helps gene-level read assignment and
transcript discovery, and degrades isoform-level quantification by spreading
reads across near-identical models [@monzo2025challenges].

That is the state of the field. The catalogues can now observe more than they
can justify including, and each use needs its own decision about which
observations belong in a reference at all.
